Dose-response effects of microaeration on thermophilic 
lignocellulose-based anaerobic digestion: performance, stability and 
microbial community dynamics

A B S T R A C T
Microaeration has emerged as a promising strategy for enhancing anaerobic digestion (AD) of lignocellulosic 
biomass, although inconsistent results highlight the need for further study. This study tested three different 
aeration rates (1, 5 and 8 mLO2/gVS) on anaerobic co-digestion of wheat straw and cattle manure under ther­
mophilic conditions (55 ◦C) in continuous-stirred tank reactors with working volume of 60 L. Daily injection of 5 
mLO2/gVS achieved the highest methane yield, with a 20.6% increase compared to the non-aerated control 
digester. Under these conditions, cellulose and hemicellulose degradation reached maximum levels of 75% and 
66.3%, respectively. In the microaerated digester, remarkable changes in microbial population were observed. 
Injection of 1 mLO2/gVS and 5 mLO2/gVS increased the relative abundance of Lentimicrobium, Turicibacter, and 
unclassified MBA03 as well as hydrogenotrophic Methanothermobacter which could contribute to enhanced 
lignocellulose degradation and biogas generation. At the final and highest oxygen dose (8 mLO2/gVS), methane 
yield began to gradually decrease. Under these conditions, the microbial profile shifted back to that of the non- 
aerated digester, suggesting that the activity of certain microbial groups was inhibited. These findings highlight 
the potential of controlled microaeration to enhance both methane yield and lignocellulosic degradation at larger 
scales, offering valuable insights for optimizing AD processes.
1. Introduction
The annual generation of agricultural biomass amounts to 5.5 billion 
tons, and due to its high availability, it is an attractive and reliable 
feedstock for anaerobic digestion (AD) (Archana et al., 2024). In recent 
years, agricultural biogas production has emerged as a favorable strat­
egy for generating alternative energy while reducing greenhouse gas 
(GHG) emissions (Møller et al., 2022). Consequently, it has a positive 
impact on the climate and environment, while AD process also yields 
valuable digestate, which supports nutrient recycling (Jasi´nska et al., 
2023; Vaneeckhaute et al., 2013). However, using agricultural waste as 
a substrate for AD poses several challenges. Agricultural biomass is often 
rich in lignocellulose, whose complex and recalcitrant structure hinders 
efficient biogas production. Lignocellulosic biomass consists of poly­
saccharides like cellulose and hemicellulose embedded in a lignin ma­
trix, forming a highly complex three-dimensional structure that impedes 
the hydrolysis step during AD (Manyi-Loh et al., 2013). The crystallinity 
of cellulose and the complexity of lignin (as an aromatic polymer) pose 
another barrier hindering the biodegradation efficiency in AD systems 
(Millati et al., 2020).
Pre-treatment is often applied before subjecting lignocellulosic 
feedstock to AD. To date, various pre-treatment methods have been 
explored to enhance lignocellulose-based AD, including alkaline or acid 
treatment, steam explosion, and ozonation (Karthikeyan et al., 2024), as

well as hyper-thermophilic AD (Kozera et al., 2024). Although these pre- 
treatment techniques can yield good results, they have specific draw­
backs, such as high energy and/or chemical consumption, inhibitory 
effects, and challenges in scaling up the process. These limitations can 
hinder commercial biogas production due to negative economic returns 
or adverse environmental impacts due to the release of inhibitory by- 
products (Xu et al., 2021).
In recent years, microaeration has gained increased interest as an 
attractive strategy for enhancing the AD process. Microaeration, defined 
as the introduction of small quantities of oxygen or air into an AD sys­
tem, has been reported as a promising technology with a positive impact 
on overall methane yield (Zeb et al., 2022), and stabilization of the 
process (Nguyen et al., 2019). Additionally, microaerobic conditions 
play a key role in hydrogen sulfide (H2S) removal during AD (Andreides 
et al., 2021). Microaerobic conditions can also alter the diversity and 
abundance of microbial communities, particularly hydrolytic bacteria 
(Fu et al., 2016) leading to increased enzymatic activity of extracellular 
hydrolytic enzymes (e.g., cellulases, xylanases, lipases). This enhance­
ment improves the hydrolysis of complex materials such as lignocellu­
lose (Duarte et al., 2018; Nguyen and Khanal, 2018). In that sense, 
applying microaeration can facilitate the AD process by creating a 
unique environment that supports the coexistence of facultative mi­
crobes and obligate anaerobes. In this setup, facultative microorganisms 
consume trace amounts of oxygen for hydrolytic processes, while pre­
serving anaerobic conditions for obligate anaerobic microbes (Fu et al., 
2023).
Despite its potential, some studies reported no improvement or even 
adverse effects of the microaeration on AD performance (Díaz et al., 
2011a; Fdz.-Polanco et al., 2009). In a study by Tsapekos et al. (2021), 
low and high oxygen loads (5 and 15 mLO2/gVS) were single-injected 
into the working volume of the reactor on daily basis for 35 days and 
resulted in positive (+10%) and negative (−4%) impact on batch AD 
tests, respectively. However, the injection of 7.3 mLO2/gVS improved 
the methane yield by 7% on continuous mode. In the continuous mode, 
the microaeration was done after the adaptation process lasting 15 days 
and was performed utilizing a single injection of oxygen into the 
working volume of the continuous-stirred tank reactor (CSTR) every day 
for 30 days. These results vary because of different aeration strategies as 
well as environmental and operating conditions in AD.
In most cases, microaeration of AD has been investigated at 
laboratory-scale (Amin et al., 2021; Cao et al., 2022; Zhu et al., 2022), 
and only a few studies reported the application of microaeration on an 
industrial-scale but mainly with a focus on H2S removal from a head­
space of the reactors (Huertas et al., 2020; Jeníˇcek et al., 2017; Muller 
et al., 2024). In that sense, microaeration technology has not yet been 
fully explored and conflicting results cannot indicate the exact under­
lying mechanism for an improved AD process. Hence, the investigation 
of the process on a larger scale may potentially help in its better un­
derstanding since it is still under development (Chen et al., 2020); 
(Krayzelova et al., 2015a) and might fill some knowledge gaps in terms 
of affecting factors or operational conditions. Furthermore, the 
microaeration treatment on larger scale has been done so far mostly by 
subjecting liquid substrates to the AD system such as high-solid waste­
water (Duangmanee et al., 2007), primary sludge (Nghiem et al., 2014), 
and wastewater ((Niu et al., 2016); (Pokorna-Krayzelova et al., 2018)). 
Thus, the utilization of agricultural wastes i.e. lignocellulosic materials 
in the large scale microaeration is attractive as it can extend the 
knowledge about the process on its impacts on solid substrates as well.
The diversity in microaeration implementation along with many 
knowledge gaps in the literature calls for further investigation to shed 
light on lignocellulose-based AD processes. To the best of authors' 
knowledge, there are only few studies reporting the impact of microa­
eration on lignocellulose-based AD which are limited to small 
laboratory-scale. Due to the potential of microaeration to enhance the 
hydrolysis rate with no adverse effect on the AD process, more investi­
gation in this field is crucial to expand and promote its application on a 
larger scale. Thus, the present work tested three different microaeration 
conditions in an anaerobic digester with a 60 L working volume, fed 
with lignocellulosic feedstock, and provided new insights into AD pro­
cess dynamics and microbial community changes. This study hypothe­
sized that controlled microaeration can enhance hydrolysis efficiency 
and stabilize the AD process without compromising biogas production. 
The primary objectives were to evaluate the impact of different 
microaeration strategies on process performance, assess microbial 
community shifts, and identify optimal conditions for scaling up 
lignocellulose-based AD.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Feedstock and inoculum
Wheat straw (WS) was harvested locally in Oostkamp, Belgium, and 
shredded to particle size <1 cm with a cutter mill. Cattle manure (CM) 
was collected from a dairy farm in Adinkerke, Belgium, and stored at 
4 ◦C before further use. Both shredded wheat straw (SWS) and CM were 
then used as feedstock for the AD experiments. The inoculum was 
sourced from a thermophilic agro-industrial biogas installation in Pit­
tem, Belgium. The characteristics of the feedstock and the inoculum are 
given in Table 1.
2.2. Experimental design and set-up
2.2.1. Digesters operational conditions
The anaerobic co-digestion experiments were conducted under 
thermophilic conditions (54 ± 1 ◦C) using two single-stage continuous 
stirred-tank reactors (CSTR) with working volume of 60 L. One of the 
digesters was utilized to perform micro-aeration treatment whereas the 
second one was used as the control (referred later in the paper as MA and 
CON, respectively). Thermophilic conditions were selected due to faster 
organic breakdown, especially complex materials e.g. agricultural 
wastes, than under mesophilic conditions (Labatut et al., 2014). The 
hydraulic retention time (HRT) was 30 days and the organic loading rate 
(OLR) for each reactor was 2.70 ± 0.10 gVS/L/day. Initially, the OLR 
was 3.40 gVS/L/d but due to operational issues observed in the begin­
ning and to avoid overfeeding, it was decreased. The mixing ratio of SWS 
and CM was 40:60 (VS basis) to provide more balanced nutrients and 
buffering capacity throughout the process (Krishania et al., 2013; Z. 
Song and Zhang, 2015). CM was selected as a co-substrate due to diverse 
microbial communities, which can readily adjust to varying operational 
circumstances. In addition, CM was noted as a material containing 
readily degradable organic matter that boosts microbial activity, facili­
tating disruption of lignocellulose recalcitrance of wheat straw (Kadam 
et al., 2023). Hence, CM and SWS was co-digested to provide improved 
process performance leading to higher, and more stable methane pro­
duction through synergy.

Continuous mixing of the reactors was provided by a central shaft 
with a propeller at the center and the bottom, rotating at 60 rpm. The 
experiment ran for 92 days and was divided into two phases. The first 
phase is called the adaptation period involving the first 21 days of start- 
up in which no aeration was applied (Period 0); followed by the lowest 
dose of air injection between days 22–44 (Period 1). The second phase 
involves the injection of higher air doses (Period 2 and Period 3) into the 
AD system between days 45–66 and 67–92, respectively, and referred as 
the experimental phase of the study. The adaptation period was done to 
acclimatize the microbial community to microaeration and the real in­
fluence of microaeration was evaluated by the results obtained in the 
experimental phase (Periods 2–3). The details of the microaeration are 
described in Section 2.2.2.
Biogas production was daily recorded in both reactors employing a 
Ritter Drum-Type Gas Meter TG0.5/0.4 mbar (Ritter Apparatebau 
GmbH & Co. KG, Bochum, Germany) with measuring range of 1–60 L/h. 
The gas composition was measured every day by utilizing a portable 
BIOGAS 5000 analyzer (Chelmsford, UK). The analyzer was connected 
to the reactor gas outlet to measure methane and carbon dioxide con­
centrations, and a single measurement lasted at least 40 s. Gas compo­
sition was normalized to 100%, assuming that only significant 
components in the dry biogas are methane and carbon dioxide. To 
monitor the stability of the AD process, samples of digestate from each 
reactor were collected once a week for pH, total solids (TS), volatile 
solids (VS), volatile fatty acids (VFA), and ammonium‑nitrogen (NH4
+-N) 
content.
2.2.2. Microaeration treatment
To provide an efficient microaeration treatment, one of the CSTR's 
was re-designed and equipped with a U-shape metal pipe with three 
perforations (diameter ~ 1 mm) at the bottom. The illustrative scheme 
of the micro-aerated reactor (MA) is shown in Fig. 1. The air pump was 
connected to the flow meter to supply accurate portion of air through the 
inlet port. Then the air was distributed into the reactor through the U- 
shape pipe. The pipe was attached to the inlet port and sealed at the end 
to provide equal air distribution inside the reactor. The end of the pipe 
was also attached to the side of the biogas outlet not to tamper with the 
headspace of the reactor which might affect the biogas composition. The 
air was injected through the inlet port and released at the bottom of the 
pipe through perforations.
Three different doses of oxygen (1, 5 and 8 mLO2/gVS per day) were 
tested. The choice of doses was inspired by the investigations of Zeb 
et al. (2022) and Tsapekos et al. (2017). They reported the aeration dose 
of around 5 mLO2/gVS as the rate with the highest enhancement in 
biogas production, and 10 mLO2/gVS as a rate leading to instability of 
AD process at lab-scale. The air was injected into the reactor once a day 
after feeding using air pump Tom&Co Aqua Bubble 33 (Tom& Co, 
London, UK). The air injection was controlled by a gas flowmeter SHLLJ 
LZQ-7 (Yuyao Shunhuan Flowmeter Co., Zhejiang, China) which was 
steadily set up at 1 L/min. The oxygen dosing strategy was calculated 
based on predetermined aeration rates for each experimental period.

2.3. Analytical methods
The pH was measured using pH meter Eutech PCD 6500 (Thermo 
Fisher Scientific Inc., Waltham, MA, USA). The TS was determined as the 
residual after placing the pre-weighed samples of feedstocks and 
digestates for 24 h drying in hot-air oven at 105 ◦C (Aronsson et al., 
2022). The VS was determined as the difference between the dry weight 
and the inorganic content, obtained by placing the dry weight in a 
muffle oven at 550 ◦C for 4 h (APHA, 2012). The TKN was measured via 
the Kjeldahl method via destruction, steam distillation, and titration 
employing Foss Kjeltec™ 8400 (Foss, Hillerød, Denmark). The ammo­
nium‑nitrogen (NH4 + -N) was determined by steam distillation 
employing Gerhardt Vapodest 20 (C. Gerhardt GmbH & Co.KG, 
K¨onigswinter, Germany) and titrimetric method utilizing 718 Stat 
Titrino (Metholm AG, Herisau, Switzerland) (InnoLab, 2021a). VFAs 
concentrations were analyzed by gas chromatography (GC) with a flame 
ionization detector-GC-FID Trace 1300 GC (Thermo Fisher Scientific 
Inc., Waltham, MA, USA) (InnoLab, 2021b). The VFA concentrations 
were calculated as chemical oxygen demand (COD) equivalents. The 
COD equivalents were adopted from elsewhere (Atasoy et al., 2020) and 
were 1.067 gCOD /g acid for acetic acid, 1.514 gCOD /g acid for pro­
pionic acid, 1.818 gCOD /g acid for isobutyric and butyric acids, 2.039 
gCOD /g acid for isovaleric and valeric acids, 2.207 gCOD /g acid for 
caproic acid. The analyses were done in triplicate for feedstocks and 
inoculum characteristics, however the samples of digestates taken once 
a week for process monitoring were analyzed in a single replicate. Fiber 
analysis was performed using the filter bag system under pressurization 
employing ANKOM DELTA Fiber Analyzer (ANKOM® Technology, Mac­
edon, NY, USA). The neutral detergent fiber (NDF) as well as acid 
detergent fiber (ADF) analysis was done following the operator's 
manual. Acid-detergent lignin (ADL) was done manually by soaking the 
bags in 72% H2SO4 for 3 h as reported by Van Soest et al., 1991. 
Additionally, the bags were ash-corrected following the method found in 
Silva et al., 2018. Each sample was analyzed in triplicate, and the fiber 
analysis was done sequentially.
2.4. Microbial community analysis
Samples from the sludge used as inoculum, and from day 21, day 44, 
day 66 and 92 in both CON and MA digesters were extracted using 
PowerSoilPro (QiaGen) with a beat-beating step of 5 × 4000 rpm for 15″ 
with 45″ intervals using a PowerLyzer instrument (QiaGen). The DNA 
was eluted in 100 μL elution buffer. 10 μL genomic DNA extract was sent 
out to LGC genomics GmbH (Berlin, Germany) for library preparation 
and sequencing on an Illumina Miseq platform with v3 chemistry with 
the primers 341F (5’-CCT ACG GGN GGC WGC AG -3’) and 785Rmod 
(5’-GAC TAC HVG GGT ATC TAA KCC-3’) (Klindworth et al., 2013).
The DADA2 R package was used to process the amplicon sequence 
data according to the pipeline tutorial (Callahan et al., 2016). In the first 
quality control step, the primer sequences were removed, and reads 
were truncated at a quality score cut-off (truncQ = 2). Besides trimming, 
additional filtering was performed to eliminate reads containing any 
ambiguous base calls or reads with high expected errors (maxEE = 2,2). 
After dereplication, unique reads were further denoised using the Divi­
sive Amplicon Denoising Algorithm (DADA) error estimation algorithm 
and the selfConsist sample inference algorithm (with the option pooling 
= TRUE). The obtained error rates were inspected and after approval, 
the denoised reads were merged.
Finally, the ASV table obtained after chimera removal was used for 
taxonomy assignment using the Naive Bayesian Classifier and the 
DADA2 formatted Silva v138.1 (Quast et al., 2013). Alpha diversity of 
the 16S rRNA marker gene was calculated using the inverse Simpson 
index, beta diversity was calculated using Bray–Curtis distances and 
PCoA was used to make ordination plots. The relative abundances of the 
top bacteria and archaea genera were selected to study specific dy­
namics in the most abundant genera (Beterams et al., 2022).
2.5. Mass balance
A mass balance was performed on each reactor to determine the 
efficacy of each applied aeration rate in fiber biodegradation during the 
whole micro aeration treatment. The efficacy of lignocellulose decom­
position refers to the degradation levels which were calculated as a 
relative value measuring the difference between the initial and final 
concentration of a specific component as a percentage (Eq. (2)) and were 
calculated for TS, VS and main lignocellulose constituents i.e. fraction of 
hemicellulose, cellulose, and lignin.

2.6. Statistics
The average values and standard deviations were calculated for key 
monitored parameters, including methane and carbon dioxide relative 
concentrations, hydrogen sulfide concentrations, biogas and methane 
yields, and fiber constituents' content. To define statistically significant 
differences (p < 0.05) among experimental measurements, a two-sided 
student t-test for two independent groups was done utilizing MS Excel 
calculation program. In addition, principal component analysis (PCA) 
was done for each experiment period to indicate dose-relationship ef­
fects of microaeration on the process. The PCA analysis was performed 
using R program.
3. Results
3.1. Impact of microaeration on biogas production and methane yield
Daily biogas and methane yields of the MA and CON digesters are 
shown in Fig. 2a and b, respectively, and the calculated biogas and 
methane yields are given in Table 3. Methane generation in the first 44 
days (Period 0 + Period 1) fluctuated in both digesters. In the MA 
reactor, the biogas yield varied from 230 to 614 L/kgVS per day and the 
methane yield fluctuated from 112 to 302 L/kgVS per day. Similar 
values were found in the CON digester, in which the daily biogas yields 
varied from 227 to 545 L/kgVS and the methane yields ranged between 
117 and 313 L/kgVS. In this period, no significant difference in biogas 
and methane production was observed (p > 0.05). The shifts in biogas 
and methane production in this adaptation period could be caused by 
changes in operational conditions at the beginning of the experiment 
during which the OLR value lowered from 3.40 to 2.70 gVS/L per day.

3.2. Impact of microaeration on digestion stability
The stability of the microaeration treatment was assessed by 
comparing the selected process parameters in both reactors as given in 
Table 4. Microaeration treatment did not influence the overall conven­
tional AD process parameters like TS, VS, pH, and TAN. TS and VS 
content remained stable throughout the whole experiment and equaled 
5.89 ± 0.13%, 5.96 ± 0.16%, and 75.5 ± 0.94%, 74.6 ± 1.20% TS for 
the MA and the CON reactors respectively. The pH value in the MA 
reactor varied from 8.08 to 8.22 and was similar to the range of pH 
observed in the CON reactor (8.06–8.21). In the case of TAN concen­
trations, it was noted that the concentration slightly increased in both 
digesters. However, they also remained at relatively constant levels and

3.3. Impact of microaeration on microbial communities
Microbial population analysis is a crucial factor in assessing 
microaeration treatment's potential for AD. Starting with an inoculum 
predominantly composed of the phyla Pseudomonadota (ex-Proteobac­
teria) (34%) and Thermotogota (34%), both digesters selected for 
Bacillota (ex-Firmicutes) among bacteria, increasing their proportion 
from 21% in the inoculum to 63% and 61% for CON and MA respectively 
(Period 0). Similarly, the proportion of archaea increased to 13 and 14% 
from an initial 3% in the inoculum. This shift, observed after 21 days 
(Period 0), can be attributed to the anaerobic conditions that drastically 
reduced the proportion of the aerobic Pseudomonas (only representative 
of the Proteobacteria) to 0.2 and 0.4% in CON and MA, respectively. 
Thermotogota were affected to a lesser extent, remaining at 13% in both 
digesters. These changes were linked to an increase in overall microbial 
diversity, as reflected in the Inverse Simpson index, which rose from 
7.67 in the inoculum to 22.3 and 28.2 in CON and MA, respectively 
(Table S2). This increased diversity is primarily due to Bacillota growth, 
dominated by unclassified MBA03 by the end of Period 1 (15 and 9% in 
CON and MA, respectively). Unclassified MBA03 has been identified 
recently as key player in anaerobic digesters (Otto et al., 2024; Puchol- 
Royo et al., 2023). The increased diversity was also due to the devel­
opment of archaea and especially of Methanosarcina, Meth­
anothermobacter and, to a lesser extent, Methanobrevibacter. These

Beta diversity analysis highlighted the growing dissimilarity of the 
two populations over time. The Principal Component Analysis (PCA) 
showed the dominant effect of time on the bacterial community in both 
CON and MA digesters (Fig. S2), with three major clusters emerging of 
this analysis: i) Period 0 samples, ii) Periods 1 and 2 samples, and iii) 
Period 3 samples. These results indicate that temporal factors outweigh 
microaeration pressure in driving community differences.
The analysis of the population dynamics (see Fig. 3) showed a 
consistent selection of unclassified MBA03 (approximately 20% in both 
digesters by the end of Period 3) and stable proportions of fermentative 
genera from the Clostridia class, including Clostridium sensu stricto, 
O_DTU014, Paeniclostridium and Romboutsia. Lentimicrobium and Turici­
bacter were also notable, exceeding 7% of total genera at the end of 
Period 3. The roles and implications of these genera are discussed in 
Section 4. In addition to the general trend of microbial community 
evolution over time, the injection of oxygen during Period 1 (1 mLO2/ 
gVS) had a significant effect on specific genera. Unclassified MBA03 
exhibited a 200% increase in MA, compared to a 50% increase in CON. 
This increase can be associated with the representation of the hydro­
genotrophic Methanothermobacter, which more than doubled in MA (8%) 
compared to CON (3%) following Period 1. Further increases in oxygen 
flow rate to 5 mLO2/gVS by the end of Period 2 reinforced this trend, 
with significantly higher proportions of unclassified MBA03 (22 versus 
13%) and Methanothermobacter (10 versus 6%) in MA compared to CON. 
Thus, certain microbial groups were promoted under microaeration 
conditions at 5 mLO2/gVS during Period 2, leading to enhanced 
methane yield and lignocellulose degradation. In contrast, the microbial 
community profile in the aerated digester during Period 3 resembled 
that of the non-aerated digester. This suggests that the activity of certain 
microbial genera may have been inhibited under these conditions, 
indicating that oxygen tolerance during microaeration narrowed at 
doses up to 8 mLO2/gVS.
Among all the genera identified, no significant presence of known 
sulfur-reducing bacteria (SRB) was detected throughout the experiment 
(<1%). However, Defluviitoga, a putative SRB (Hania et al., 2012), was 
the main representative of the Thermotogota phylum. Its proportion 
decreased over time in both CON and MA reactors, dropping from 7% 
and 6% in Period 1 to 2% in Period 2 and further to 1% in Period 3, 
respectively. This decline suggests that microbial production of H2S 
occurred in both digesters and explains the significant reduction in H₂S 
levels between Periods 1 and 2/3 (Table 3).
The microaeration conditions likely inhibited Defluviitoga activity, 
contributing to the observed rapid decrease in H₂S concentrations in the 
MA reactor (Fig. S1), as shown by Gutierrez et al., 2008. However, this 
inhibition does not appear to be the primary factor driving the decrease 
in Defluviitoga abundance, as a similar trend was observed in the CON 
reactor. Additionally, no notable abundance of sulfur-oxidizing bacteria 
(SOB) was detected (<1%), indicating that no significant microbial 
mitigation of H₂S occurred in the MA reactor compared to the CON 
reactor.
3.4. Dose-response effects of microaeration on the AD process
The Principal Component Analysis (PCA) was done to assess dose- 
response relationships between process performance and microbial 
community kinetics across three microaeration conditions (Fig. 4). The 
results revealed distinct patterns of microbial-performance links that 
evolved with increasing doses of oxygen. During Period 1, the confi­
dence ellipses for MA and CON clusters depicted substantial overlap that 
indicates no remarkable differentiation at this low oxygen dose. This 
corresponds to no significant differences in methane yield and fiber 
degradation. On the other hand, in Period 2, the most pronounced 
separation between MA and CON samples was observed. The MA_D2 
samples clustered in the positive region of PC1, strongly associated with

In general, the PCA results clearly demonstrate that microaeration 
under optimal dosing strategy with 5 mLO2/gVS creates distinct mi­

was mostly driven by the boost of syntrophic acetate-oxidizing bacteria 
(unclassified MBA03) and hydrogenotrophic Methanothermobacter, 
which facilitated improved lignocellulose degradation and methane 
generation. The clear spatial separation of MA and CON samples along 
with the strong association between methane yield and key microbial 
genera, gives quantitative evidence that 5 mLO2/gVS demonstrates the 
optimal microaeration rate for thermophilic anaerobic co-digestion of 
LCB.
4. Discussion
This study investigated three different microaeration rates (1, 5, and 
8 mLO2/gVS) to assess the feasibility of microaerobic treatment on large 
lab-scale for enhanced methane production and lignocellulose hydro­
lysis. Each aeration rate was evaluated for approximately one HRT. 
According to Holliger et al. (2016), stable digestion can be assumed 
when measured parameters (e.g. biogas production, VFA, VS, pH) are 
consistently maintained within 10% of their average values for a mini­
mum period of one HRT. In our study, the results demonstrate stable 
process performance with consistent key parameters (Table 4). It con­
firms the system had reached operational stability within each evalua­
tion period.
The results revealed that the injection of 1 mLO2/gVS into the 
reactor during the adaptation period did not influence the AD perfor­
mance and ran similarly to the conventional AD process. This finding 
conflicts with some previous reports, for example, (Zhu et al., 2022) 
reported an enhancement of 7.8% in methane yield with a single in­
jection of oxygen load of 0.2 mLO2/gVS while performing AD of corn 
straw. However, the difference might be related to the scale of the ex­
periments. The enhancement was obtained under small lab-scale con­
ditions utilizing shaking air bath with the shaking speed of 200 rpm. 
That could potentially provide better operational conditions for oxygen 
distribution inside the reactor and enhanced the overall performance of 
the AD when compared to larger digesters. This indicates the necessity of

Even though the aeration rate of 1 mLO2/gVS resulted in no signif­
icant impact on enhanced methane yield, remarkable differences in 
methane generation were observed during the following periods. The 
highest methane yield enhancement was obtained with an oxygen load 
of 5 mLO2/gVS and amounted to 20%. A slightly lower increase (16%) 
was noted when 8 mLO2/gVS was employed. These results tie well with 
previous studies wherein the methane yield was increased by 7.2%, 
injecting the load of oxygen of 5 mLO2/gVS for consecutive 3-day 
treatment during the AD of wheat straw (Tsapekos et al., 2017). A 
similar conclusion was reached by Fu et al. (2015) who reported that 
microaerobic pretreatment of corn straw with the same oxygen load led 
to an enhancement of methane yield by 16% when compared to un­
treated digester. However, in both cases, microaeration was done at 
small lab-scale conditions as well and deployed as a pre-treatment of 
substrate instead of direct injection inside the digester.
In another study, Tsapekos et al. (2021) conducted microaeration 
experiment in which wheat straw was co-digested with livestock slurry 
in CSTR and reported that a load of oxygen 7.3 mLO2/gVS resulted in the 
highest enhancement of methane yield by 7%. The enhancement was 
caused by the promotion of hydrolysis during microaeration treatment 
but no remarkable changes in microbial community were observed. 
Only an increased relative abundance of aero-tolerant archaea e.g. 
Methanosarcina and Methanobacterium under microaerobic condition 
was observed which can suggest that these species contributed to in­
crease in methane generation. The same microaeration strategy was 
used by Zeb et al. (2022) and observed greatly higher methane yield 
enhancement up to 32% during the AD of buffalo manure under meso­
philic conditions on a lab scale. In that case study it was reported to 
degrade acid-soluble lignin (ASL) content by 78% which could conse­
quently enhance the availability of enzymes to decompose cellulose and 
hemicellulose that resulted in higher conversion of the substrate into 
biogas. However, in both papers, authors do not indicate a particular 
reason for enhancement in obtained methane yields. Either way, these 
results suggest that microaerobic conditions affect the methane yield 
positively but at different levels, depending on the dose of oxygen, 
operational conditions (e.g., scale, reactor configuration, frequency of 
microaeration), and choice of feedstock.
Nevertheless, our study concludes that microaeration at a flow rate 
of up to 8 mLO2/gVS positively enhanced methane yield from the AD of 
wheat straw and cattle manure. It also highlights that oxygen dosages 
used in laboratory settings can have practical applications and lead to 
significant differences in methane production on a larger scale. At 8 
mLO2/gVS/d, the microbial community shifted but remained largely 
similar to that of the non-aerated digester, suggesting that oxygen doses 
above this threshold may begin to inhibit certain microbial activity. The 
depletion of microbial activity could explain the gradual decrease in 
methane yield observed during Period 3. However, while 8 mLO2/gVS 
may still be a promising flow rate for lignocellulose-based AD, further 
investigation is required.
Another important effect of the microaeration on AD process is a 
change in H2S concentrations which is believed to be mitigated in situ by 
providing microaerobic conditions inside the digester (Krayzelova et al., 
2015b). For instance, it was observed that microaeration provided 
enhanced methane yield with simultaneous H2S mitigation from AD of 
chicken manure which generates biogas with a high concentration of 
H2S (Mahdy et al., 2020; Y. Song et al., 2020). In our study, application 
of 5 and 8 mLO2/gVS resulted in significant differences (p < 0.05) in H2S 
concentration between the MA and the CON reactors. Considering the 
average values of H2S concentration in the reactors, its content 
decreased by 16% and 9% in the MA during D2 and D3 compared to the 
untreated digester, respectively. According to Y. Song et al. (2020), a 
single injection of oxygen at 1.4 mL/gVS/d resulted in 68% H2S removal 
and was improved after the implication of continuous mode of oxygen 
injection reaching the removal level of 31–60%. It was also observed 
that continuous aeration with an oxygen load of 4.2 mL/gVS/d led to a 
removal level in the range of 91–120%. In the study of Mahdy et al. 
(2020), it was reported that H2S content decreased by ~50% after a 
single injection of 6.3 mLO2/gVS/d. Thus, it indicates that in situ 
desulfurization might be also performed when subjecting cattle manure 
and wheat straw to co-digestion but with a lower efficiency.
It is noteworthy that 5 h after the injection of air, the H2S was 
removed at the level of ~90%. However, after 24 h, its concentration 
reached the same concentration value as it was before the application of 
oxygen. Even though, the long exposure to a single injection of oxygen 
could contribute to the gradual mitigation of H2S in the biogas compo­
sition, the continuous injection of air might be necessary for its long- 
term consistent removal and should be investigated in further 
research. H2S removal found in the MA reactor might be also explained 
by the suggestion found in Song et al., 2020 which stated that enhancing 
hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis with air injection could help main­
tain lower hydrogen partial pressure and promote AD stability. Hypo­
thetically, changes in H2S concentrations could be also attributed to the 
competitive oxygen utilization by sulfur oxidizing bacteria (SOB) 
(Nghiem et al., 2014) or by the inhibition of SRB while oxygen injection 
inside the digester. Some SRB species can oxidize sulfide under aerobic 
conditions and reduce sulfate under oxic conditions (Canfield and Des 
Marais, 1991; Fuseler, 1996). However, there is no clear evidence so far 
indicating the growth of SRB under these conditions. On the other hand, 
in our study, among all the genera identified, no significant presence of 
SRB or SOB were detected which makes this hypothesis doubtful. 
Alternatively, the phenomenon can be related to the limited solubility of 
pure oxygen in water. The injected air could consequently transfer 
through the liquid fraction and interact with rich H2S biogas in the 
headspace of the digester. Then, the temporary changes in H2S con­
centrations could have been mitigated due to the biochemical or 
chemical oxidation process (Díaz et al., 2011b; Ramos et al., 2012) 
Summing up, the exact metabolic pathway of sulfide conversion and 
oxidation under microaerobic conditions is still poorly understood 
(Krayzelova et al., 2015a) and it is challenging to indicate only one 
underlying mechanism responsible for H2S removal under microaera­
tion treatment.
The degradation level of lignin fraction was constant in both reactors 
throughout the experiment, and no remarkable differences have been 
observed since lignin is believed to be a very recalcitrant material with a 
low level of biodegradability when subjected to the AD. Lignin decom­
position poses a very challenging task due to its complex chemical 
structure which is resistant to the AD process and might require addi­
tional treatment that will be combined with microaeration strategy. For 
example, Akyol et al. (2019) revealed that fungal pre-treatment of 
lignocellulosic biomass with Trametes versicolor improved methane yield 
by 10–18% and cellulose degradation up to 80%. In the mentioned 
study, fungal treatment and aerobic conditions provided favorable 
conditions for lignin decomposition leading to increased presence of 
specific hydrolytic enzymes and consequently resulting in enhanced 
lignocellulosic breakdown. It suggests that combined treatment should 
be also taken into consideration in future.
Microaerobic conditions have been reported to facilitate the abun­
dance of hydrolytic bacteria (Fu et al., 2016) whose enzymatical activ­
ities might lead to improved hydrolysis of complex biomass such as 
lignocellulose (Duarte et al., 2018; Nguyen and Khanal, 2018). An 
example of the functional consortia that can hydrolyze polysaccharides 
in lignocellulose i.e. hemicellulose and cellulose are the phyla Bacillota 
and Bacteroidetes (Hanreich et al., 2013). The relative abundance of 
both phyla has been also reported to increase under microaerobic con­
ditions (Fu et al., 2016; Zhu et al., 2022) creating a unique microbial 
population permitting coexistence of facultative microbes and obligate 
anaerobic microorganisms (Fu et al., 2023). In our study, the enhance­
ment of relative abundance of phyla Bacillota was observed (see Fig. 3) 
which potentially contributed to increased degradation levels of

The genera identified in the final sample (after Period 3) are

The various genera of Clostridia present are likely involved in oxidizing 
resulting molecules into acetate (and CO2) while producing H2. Subse­
quently, unclassified MBA03, identified as a syntrophic acetate-oxidizing 
bacterium (SAOB) (Dyksma et al., 2020), completes the oxidation of 
acetate and other volatile fatty acids (VFA) into CO2, making it available 
for hydrogenotrophic methanogens.
This analysis suggests that improving AD performance could involve 
enrichment strategies focused on genera such as Lentimicrobium or 
Turicibacter, which are significantly represented and likely responsible 
for degrading complex organic compounds. Enhancing their activity 
could optimize the utilization of lignocellulose-based substrates.
5. Conclusion
Microaeration of a lignocellulose-based anaerobic digester at a 
single-injection rate of 5 mLO2/gVS resulted in the highest methane 
yield and the greatest degradation of hemicellulose and cellulose. These 
conditions increased the relative abundance of hydrogenotrophic 
methanogens (Methanothermobacter) and SAOB (unclassified MBA03), 
which may have facilitated a shift from acetoclastic methanogenesis to 
hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis due to syntrophic acetate oxidation. 
This shift, in turn, contributed to in situ H2S removal. Additionally, the 
results demonstrated that microaeration at 5 mLO2/gVS significantly 
influenced the microbial community, promoting the growth of Lentimi­
crobium, Turicibacter.Based on these findings, controlled microaerobic 
conditions can be practically applied to lignocellulose-based AD at a 
larger scale without adverse effects on the process. However, the authors 
suggest further investigation considering a continuous dosing of oxygen 
prior to an upscaled implementation.
